references.text: The context for Jesus' prayer struggle in Gethsemane. Jesus had gone to the Mount of Olives and asked the disciples to pray so that they would not fall into temptation ([ref:Luk 22:39-40|Luke 22:39-40]).

The parallel account in Matthew where Jesus finds the disciples sleeping, wakes them, and finds them asleep again ([ref:Matt 26:40-43|Matthew 26:40-43]). Matthew notes that "the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak".
The parallel account in Mark where Jesus finds the disciples sleeping three times during prayer in Gethsemane ([ref:Mark 14:37-40|Mark 14:37-40]). Mark mentions that "their eyes were heavy".
Matthew specifically states that the disciples slept "because their eyes were heavy" ([ref:Matt 26:43|Matthew 26:43]), a parallel to Luke's explanation that they slept because of sorrow.
Jesus had predicted that the disciples' hearts would be filled with sorrow (λύπη) ([ref:Joh 16:6|John 16:6]), the same Greek word used in Luke 22:45 regarding why they fell asleep.

Jesus speaks of the disciples' sorrow (λύπη) that is coming, but which will be turned into joy ([ref:Joh 16:20-22|John 16:20-22]). The sorrow the disciples experienced in Gethsemane was linked to their awareness of Jesus' impending suffering.
At the transfiguration on the mountain, Jesus also found the disciples weighed down by sleep ([ref:Luk 9:32|Luke 9:32]). A similar pattern where the disciples fall asleep at critical moments.
The immediately following verse where Jesus wakes them and again urges them to pray so that they will not fall into temptation ([ref:Luk 22:46|Luke 22:46]).

Jonah was found in deep sleep in the midst of a crisis ([ref:Jona 4:8|Jonah 1:5-6]). An example from the Old Testament of sleeping during a time of serious danger, just as the disciples slept in Gethsemane.
"A glad heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones" ([ref:Ordsp 17:22|Proverbs 17:22]). The sorrow may have physically exhausted the disciples so that they fell asleep.
